did_you_know.text: Did you know? Zechariah presents the Lord as the source of rain and growth: he makes lightning and gives rain to everyone, with vegetation in the field. Therefore, the people are called to ask him for rain at the time of the spring rains—the rains at the end of the season.

Did you know? The chapter contrasts the word of the Lord with sources of deception: the household idols speak falsehood, the diviners see lies, and worthless dreams offer empty comfort. As a result, the people wander like sheep without a shepherd.

Did you know? The Lord announces that his anger burns against the “shepherds” and the “leaders.” Throughout the chapter, the images of sheep and shepherds describe failed leadership that has left the people without direction.

Did you know? From the house of Judah will come four images of strength and stability: a cornerstone, a tent peg, a war bow, and every ruler. Together, they portray a people capable of building, defending themselves, and fighting.

Did you know? Judah’s strength is described as the result of the Lord’s presence: they will be like warriors trampling through the mud of the streets, fighting and, by doing so, putting their enemies’ horsemen to shame.
Did you know? The promise is not limited to the house of Judah: the Lord promises to strengthen the house of Judah and save the house of Joseph, restoring them because he has compassion on them.

Did you know? Ephraim’s joy is described as the joy of wine, and it includes their children as well: they will see and rejoice, and their hearts will be glad in the Lord. In this way, redemption is portrayed as both a family and a national celebration.

Did you know? The Lord describes the gathering of his people with the image of a whistle or call that draws them to him. They will be gathered because he has redeemed them, and they will become numerous.

Did you know? Even after being scattered among the nations, the people will remember the Lord, live with their children, and return. The chapter specifically mentions their gathering from Egypt and Assyria to the regions of Gilead and Lebanon.

Did you know? The description of redemption includes renewed control over the waters and the empires: the Lord strikes the waves of the sea, dries up the depths of the Nile, humbles Assyria’s pride, and removes Egypt’s scepter.
Did you know? The chapter’s conclusion emphasizes that this strengthening is not merely military or political: the Lord makes his people strong in him, and they walk in his name.
